We have mass spec: m/z 193.1103 (most intense). Likely molecular ion [M+H]+? Usually ESI positive gives M+H. So neutral mass ~192.102? Let's compute: 193.1103 - 1.0073 = 192.103. That corresponds to formula? Let's calculate possible formula C11H12O3: exact mass: C11=132.000, H12=12.0939, O3=47.9847 total = 192.0786. Slightly lower. C10H12O4: C10=120, H12=12.094, O4=63.9797 total = 196.0737. Not match. C9H12O5: 108+12.094+79.974=200.068. Not. C11H12O2: 132+12.094+31.9898=176.084. Not. C12H16O3: 144+16.125+47.985=208.11. Not.

Our observed mass 192.103 (neutral). Could be C11H12O3 (192.0786) difference 0.0245 (approx 125 ppm). Might be okay? Could be C10H16O4: 120+16.125+63.98=200.105. No.

Maybe the ion is [M+Na]+? 193.110 - 22.9898 = 170.1205. Not typical.

Could be [M+H]+ of C10H13O3? C10H13O3 mass: C10 120, H13 13.101, O3 47.985 = 181.086. Not.

Let's compute exact mass for C11H12O3: using monoisotopic: C 12.0000, H 1.007825, O 15.994915. So 11*12 =132. 12*1.007825=12.0939. 3*15.994915=47.984745. Sum =192.078645. Add proton 1.007276 =193.085921. Observed 193.1103, diff 0.0244 (124 ppm). Could be measurement error? Might be okay but maybe formula is C10H16O4? Let's compute: C10 120, H16 16.1252, O4 63.97966 =200.10486. +H =201.112. Not.

C9H12O5: 108+12.0939+79.9746=200.0685 +H =201.0758.

C12H12O2: 144+12.0939+31.9898=188.0837 +H =189.091. Not.

C13H12O2: 156+12.0939+31.9898=200.0837 +H =201.091.

So C11H12O3 seems plausible.

Now carbon NMR data: 11 carbons? We have 11 deltas: 166.40, 144.78, 132.00, 130.07, 130.07, 127.80, 127.80, 52.24, 49.55, 43.55, 19.23.

So 11 carbons matches formula C11.

Interpretation: 166.4 likely carbonyl (ester or acid). 144.78 aromatic quaternary. 132,130,130,127.8 aromatic CH/ quaternary. So aromatic ring with 6 carbons (maybe phenyl). Then aliphatic carbons: 52.24 (O-CH3 or O-CH2), 49.55, 43.55, 19.23 (methyl). So maybe an ethyl ester attached to aromatic? Example: methyl phenylacetate? That is C9H10O2? Not.

Our earlier guess of CCOC(=O)C1=CC=C(OC)C=C1 (ethyl 4-methoxybenzoate) formula C10H12O3 (mass 180). Not match.

We need C11H12O3: maybe methyl 4-methoxybenzoate? That's C9? Wait methyl 4-methoxybenzoate: C9? Actually benzoic acid C7H6O2, add methoxy (OCH3) gives C8H8O3? Not.

Let's compute: 4-methoxybenzoic acid (p-anisic acid) formula C8H8O3? Actually benzoic acid C7H6O2, add OCH3 substituent (adds CH3O) gives C8H8O3? plus extra O? Wait anisic acid is C8H8O3? Let's check: C6H4(OH)CO2H? Actually anisic acid is methoxybenzoic acid: C6H4(OCH3)CO2H => C8H8O3? Carbons: 6+1+1=8, hydrogens: 4 (ring) +3 (OCH3) +1 (COOH) =8, O: 3. So C8H8O3 mass 152. Not.

Our formula C11H12O3 suggests aromatic ring (6 C) plus carbonyl (C=O) plus maybe two alkyl groups (C3 each). Could be phenylpropionate? e.g., phenylpropionic acid (C9H10O2) not.

Maybe it's methyl phenylacetate (C9H10O2). Not.

Consider ethyl phenylacetate: C10H12O2? Actually phenylacetate (C8H7O2) plus ethyl adds C2H5 => C10H12O2. Not.

Our carbon NMR shows carbonyl at 166 (ester). So likely an ester. Aromatic ring with maybe methoxy (OCH3) gives O-CH3 at ~55 ppm (52.24). Good. So we have an aromatic methoxy group. Also maybe an ethyl group attached to carbonyl: O-CH2-CH3 gives CH2 at ~60 ppm, CH3 at ~14 ppm. But we have 49.55, 43.55, 19.23. 19.23 could be methyl of ethyl (CH3). 49.55 maybe CH2 attached to carbonyl (O-CH2-). 43.55 maybe carbon attached to aromatic? Not.

Alternatively, could be a benzoate with isopropyl group? Isopropyl carbon attached to O (CH) ~68, not.

Our 52.24 likely O-CH3 (methoxy). 49.55 maybe benzylic CH2 (Ph-CH2-). 43.55 maybe carbonyl carbon? No carbonyl is 166. So 43.55 maybe carbon attached to carbonyl (C=O-CH2-). 19.23 methyl attached to that carbon (CH3). So maybe structure: methyl 4-methoxyphenylacetate? That would be OCH3 on aromatic, carbonyl attached to OCH3 (methyl ester) and CH2 attached to aromatic. Let's compute formula: aromatic ring C6H4, methoxy substituent OCH3 adds C1H3O1, carbonyl carbon C1O1, ester OCH3 adds C1H3O1, CH2 bridging adds C1H2. Total C:6+1+1+1+1=10? Wait count: ring 6, methoxy carbon 1, carbonyl carbon 1, ester methyl carbon 1, benzylic CH2 carbon 1 =10. That's C10, not C11. Need extra carbon maybe ethyl ester instead of methyl: ethyl ester adds C2H5O. Then total C:6+1+1+2+1=11. Good. So ethyl 4-methoxyphenylacetate? Actually ethyl 4-methoxyphenylacetate would have OCH3 on aromatic, carbonyl attached to O-CH2-CH3 (ethyl), and CH2 attached to aromatic. Formula: C6H4 (ring) + OCH3 (C1H3O1) + CO (C1O1) + OCH2CH3 (C2H5O1) + CH2 (C1H2) = C11 H? H: ring 4, OCH3 3, OCH2CH3 5, CH2 2 =14? plus maybe carbonyl no H. So total H =4+3+5+2=14. But our formula H12. So maybe not.

Our H count 12 suggests less hydrogens. Maybe aromatic is disubstituted with two O groups, reducing H. For phenyl with two substituents (e.g., methoxy and carbonyl ester) ring hydrogens =4. So ring contributes 4 H. Add OCH3 (3 H) =7. Add ethyl ester OCH2CH3 (5 H) =12. Add benzylic CH2 (2 H) =14. Too many.

But we have only 12 H total, so maybe no ethyl, maybe methyl ester (3 H) and no benzylic CH2? Let's compute methyl 4-methoxybenzoate: ring 4 H, OCH3 3 H, methyl ester 3 H =10 H. Not 12.

Our formula C11H12O3 suggests degree of unsaturation DBE = C - H/2 + N/2 +1 = 11 -12/2 +1 = 11 -6 +1 =6. So 6 DBE. Aromatic ring accounts for 4 DBE (ring + 3 double bonds). Carbonyl adds 1. So total 5, need one more: maybe another double bond or ring. Could be a second aromatic ring? Not.

But aromatic ring (benzene) is 4 DBE. Carbonyl 1 =5. Need one more: maybe a second carbonyl (but only 3 O). Could be an ester (C=O) counts as 1 DBE. So maybe there is a second double bond (C=C) in side chain. Could be a cinnamate (phenyl with C=C-COO). That adds one DBE. So structure could be methyl p-methoxycinnamate (anisic acid derivative). Methyl p-methoxycinnamate formula: C11H12O3? Let's compute: Cinnamic acid (C9H8O2). Add methoxy on para: adds C1H3O1 => C10H11O3? Wait need to recalc. Cinnamic acid: C9H8O2 (C6H5-CH=CH-COOH). Add methoxy on ring (OCH3) adds C1H3O1, replace a hydrogen on ring, so C10H11O3? Actually H count: original ring had 5 H, after methoxy substitution reduces by 1, adds 3 from OCH3, net +2. So H becomes 8+2=10? Wait original H 8 (C9H8O2). After substitution, H becomes 8 -1 (lost ring H) +3 =10. So C10H10? Let's compute again: C9 -> +1 = C10. H8 -> -1 +3 =10. O2 -> +1 = O3. So C10H10O3. Not our formula.

Methyl ester of that: add CH3 to COOH (replace OH with OCH3). That adds C1H3 and removes H from OH (1). So net +C1 H2. So formula becomes C11H12O3. Yes! So methyl p-methoxycinnamate (also known as methyl 4-methoxycinnamate) has formula C11H12O3. Good! DBE: aromatic 4, C=C 1, carbonyl 1 =6. matches.

Now carbon NMR: carbonyl carbon ~166 (yes). Aromatic carbons: 144.78 (para carbon attached to OCH3), 132,130,130,127.8 (others). The alkene carbons: one around 132? Actually trans-alkene CH (C=CH) around 130-135. The other alkene carbon attached to carbonyl (C=O) around 144? But we already have 144.78 maybe carbonyl carbon? No carbonyl is 166. So 144 could be alkene carbon attached to carbonyl (alpha,beta-unsaturated). 132 maybe other alkene carbon attached to aromatic. The OCH3 carbon at 52.24 (methoxy). The methyl of ester at 49.55? Actually methyl of ester OCH3 is around 52 as well. But we have two O-CH3 groups: one on aromatic (methoxy) ~55, one on ester ~52. So 52.24 could be ester OCH3, 49.55 maybe aromatic OCH3? Slightly lower. 43.55 maybe CH2? But there is no CH2 in cinnamate (it's CH=CH). So 43.55 maybe something else. However we have 19.23 maybe methyl? But we already accounted for two methyls. Wait we have only two methyl groups (both OCH3). No aliphatic CH3. So 19.23 seems out of place. Could be impurity.

But overall pattern fits methyl p-methoxycinnamate.

Let's simulate spectra to verify.
